Chapter 23

The design system

Tokens with light-dark(), a theme class on MediaQuery, the boot script that stops the flash and tells the browser chrome and the server, fonts from fontsource preloaded by filename, a hero in four prints that downloads one, one GSAP timeline as an attachment, motion tokens that reduced motion zeroes, the short, named list of places a hex code may appear outside the tokens, and a contrast table checked on every lint.

By the end of this chapter

Build a light-and-dark design system that never flashes, respects reduced motion, and keeps every colour in one file.

Five CSS files, imported in order: tokens define, reset clears, base styles, the date fields’ sheet dresses what Bits UI renders, utilities lay out. dates.css is global rather than a component’s <style> because two components — the trip’s range and an expense’s single date — wear it, and the elements it styles are rendered by the library, out of reach of a scoped selector (chapter 22). Every colour, size and duration the interface uses is named once in the first, and components reference the names. A hex code anywhere else in src is a copy made where a custom property cannot be read, and there are four, each saying so where it is written: the map’s canvas (map/style.ts), the globe’s WebGL scene, the custom element’s shadow root, and the theme-color meta tags in app.html, which the browser reads before any stylesheet. The header of tokens.css lists them, along with the two hex codes that are not copies: print, which is black on white whatever the theme, and the #000 in a mask-image gradient, which means “opaque”, not black.

light-dark() is the whole theming mechanism. Each token holds its light value and its dark value and the browser picks by color-scheme, which follows the system by default and is pinned by data-theme on <html> when a person chooses. No duplicated @media (prefers-color-scheme) blocks, no .dark cascade, and — because the choice is applied before the first paint — no flash. The palette is “a map on a table, lit like a film”: warm paper in four surface tiers, ink in four weights, one teal that reads as water, and one hue per kind of stop that the itinerary and the map share through --kind-*. Three of the tokens exist only because of contrast arithmetic: --on-fill is the ink that reads on every kind colour in both themes (white fails on the pastel dark kinds at 1.9:1); the light --ink-3 was darkened until tertiary text passed 4.5:1 on every tier; and --segment-edge is the 1px edge a chosen segment draws — the theme toggle, the notes toolbar, the stop’s kind — because the tier step alone is 1.1:1 in dark and 1.2:1 in light, a state nobody can see, and the edge is 3:1 or better against both the track and the segment. The --night tokens are the one family that is not light-dark(): the globe is a night scene in both themes. The scale has eight steps, each a clamp() between a 360px phone and a 1280px desktop, with a leading and a tracking token to pair with each — big serif closes up, small serif is left alone — and most durations are a --dur-* that the prefers-reduced-motion block at the bottom sets to zero. Not all: the view transitions, the live dot’s pulse and the home page’s card stagger write their timing as numbers, and the tab indicator’s tween, the list’s flip and the map’s camera are JavaScript. Each of those sits behind a reduced-motion check of its own, and the comment above the block names every one — “reads a token” and “is switched off” are two different claims, and the second is the one that matters.

The display face is Fraunces, a variable font with an optical-size axis that the browser maps from the font size — font-optical-sizing: auto, so an 18px heading gets the cut drawn for 18px and a 56px hero gets the one drawn for posters; only the hero title pins "opsz" 144, and the 404 numeral pins 96 — at 46 to 72px the poster cut lost its hairlines and each “4” read as a blob. The body is Inter. Both come from fontsource as stylesheets of @font-face rules with unicode-range, so a browser downloads the latin subset and nothing else — and chapter 15’s preload filter names those two files by their source filename.

The theme, and the flash it prevents

MediaQuery from svelte/reactivity is the system’s preference as a reactive value: when the operating system switches at sunset, resolved changes and the toaster and the map style follow, without anybody polling. The class only decides what color-scheme is; the CSS does the work. browser from $app/env guards the storage reads, because this module is imported on the server too. Two things outside the stylesheet follow a change as well, and set() updates both: the theme-color meta tags, and a cookie for the server — the next two blocks say what each is for.

Why one instance in a module, when Svelte advises context

Svelte’s best practices prefer context to state declared in a shared module, and the reason is the server: a module is loaded once per process, so state in it is shared by every request that process renders, and one person’s value can end up in another person’s page. theme is safe from that by construction, and the comment at the top of the file says where. On the server the constructor returns before it reads anything, and set() is only called from a change handler, which never runs there — so the server’s instance is system for its whole life and holds nothing of anybody’s. The person’s choice reaches a server render by another road, as data.theme, read from the cookie for that one request. Context would be the answer the day the module held something per person on the server; until then, a singleton that is written only in the browser is the simpler honest thing.

theme-color is the colour a phone paints its status bar and a desktop browser its tab strip. It is --paper’s two values, by hand, because a <meta> is read before any stylesheet and cannot see a token. Two tags with media queries follow the system; the catch is a person who *chose* — a dark page on a light phone would sit under a cream bar. So the boot script below, and theme.set() later, point the chosen tag at every screen (media="all") and the other at none (media="not all"). Rewriting media rather than content keeps both colours in the HTML, where the comment beside them can say where they came from.

The one inline script in the app, and the reason vite.config.ts hashes it. A dark choice on a light system would otherwise paint light for one frame before hydration; this runs before the first paint, sets data-theme from storage, points the theme-color tags, and writes the choice into a cookie — the one thing the *server* needs to know about a theme, for the hero below. The variable names are one letter and the syntax is var because this is the only JavaScript that runs before the bundle, untranspiled, in every browser that loads the page. It carries no nonce attribute, because the guides are prerendered and SvelteKit refuses to prerender a template with %sveltekit.nonce% in it — the hash in script-src allows it everywhere.

A radio group, because that is what it is: one of three, always exactly one. Arrow keys move between them for free, and a screen reader says “Theme, Light, 2 of 3” with no ARIA beyond the fieldset. :has(input:checked) styles the label from the state of the input inside it, which is what :has() was made for — and what it paints is a tier-3 pill with the --segment-edge hairline, so the choice shows in the dark theme too.

A picture in four prints

The hero is a map of the sample trip drawn by scripts/make-hero.ts with sharp — coastline, contours clipped to the land, a graticule, the dashed route and its numbered pins — once on cream for the light theme and once on near-black for the dark. Drawn twice rather than filtered once: the first version developed the cream print as a negative in the dark theme, filter: invert(1) hue-rotate(180deg), and a negative is not a night map — the pins’ white numbers went black, and the land and the sea took whatever greys the arithmetic gave them rather than the night tokens’. The script is deterministic, so running it again produces the same bytes and the diff of a commit that touches it is honest.

And each print is drawn twice, for two sizes of screen. A pin and its number are drawn in the pixels of the image, and the image is shown 40rem wide on a desktop and the full width of a 360px phone: the desktop drawing’s 26px pins came out 15px across on the phone, with numbers under 5px tall. So the script draws a desktop print at 1600×1000 and a phone print at 1200×750, framed a little tighter on the route, and every size in it — strokes, pins, numbers — is written in screen pixels at the narrowest the print is shown and multiplied out per print: the phone’s pins are 21px with 11.5px numbers at 360px. The compass rose is the desktop’s ornament only; drawn on the phone print it sat on Barcelona.

Four prints must not mean four downloads, and the hero is the largest thing on the first screen — its paint *is* the page’s Largest Contentful Paint. <picture> makes the choice before any script runs: the browser takes the first <source> whose media and type match, so the order of the sources is the decision, and prints is that order as data. With no theme chosen, the night prints come first with (prefers-color-scheme: dark) in their media and the day prints follow, so the system decides. With a theme chosen, only that theme’s prints are rendered, with no colour scheme in their media, so a dark choice on a light phone fetches a night print and never a day one. Within each theme the desktop print carries (min-width: 37em) and comes first, and the phone print after it carries no width at all. 37em is not one of the layout’s breakpoints; it is where the desktop print’s numbers reach 11px — 30px of a 1600px drawing, shown about 590px wide — so below it the phone print, drawn for that, takes over. The server learns the choice from the cookie the boot script writes, through the (site) layout’s load (the next chapter quotes it); once the page is running, the live choice takes over, so flipping the toggle on this page swaps the print.

Why running, and not theme.choice from the start

The first render in the browser is hydration, and hydration does not draw the page again: it walks the elements the server sent and attaches to them, so it has to describe the same markup the server wrote. The server knew the choice only from the cookie, as data.theme. Read theme.choice straight away and a person whose storage and cookie disagree — another tab changed the theme a moment ago — describes different <source>s from the ones in the document. Where only a srcset differs Svelte keeps the server’s and ignores its own; where the number of sources differs hydration fails, and Svelte throws the server’s page away and renders all of it again. So the first render reads data.theme, as the server did; onMount runs once hydration is done and sets running, and from then on the live choice decides. The general rule is worth keeping: a value only the browser knows may change the page *after* hydration, never during it.

All four prints are ?enhanced imports with the widths named — the same pipeline as <enhanced:img>, run by the preprocessor that must come first in vite.config.ts: AVIF and WebP at four widths for a desktop print and three for a phone print, with the intrinsic width and height known so nothing shifts while it loads — the phone print is 16:10 like the desktop’s, so the one <img> reserves the right space for either. The component is not used because it cannot put a media on a source; the import gives the same sources and img and the markup is written by hand, with src/images.d.ts telling TypeScript what such an import returns. Each source’s sizes tells the browser how wide that print is on screen — 40rem from 64em or the whole width for a desktop print, the whole width for a phone print — so it picks the smallest file that is still sharp, and fetchpriority="high" says it is the one to fetch first. On a phone the image steps out of the gutter to the screen’s edges and its bottom edge fades into the paper — only the bottom: a fade at the top as well left the map a faint band with dead space under it.

Why a cookie, when the choice is already in storage

Because the server renders the <picture>, and the browser starts fetching an image from the HTML long before any script could change it. localStorage is invisible to the server; a cookie is sent with the request. The cookie is a mirror, not a second source of truth: every colour still comes from light-dark() and data-theme, so a missing or stale cookie costs at most one picture drawn for the other theme — never a flash, never a wrong colour on anything else.

One timeline, four rules

The project’s cinematic budget is spent on the globe and on one hero. Everything else moves the way a good editor cuts: rarely, and for a reason — a dialog rises 8px, a bottom sheet slides on the iOS curve, a tab indicator is a Tween from svelte/motion, the check mark on a copy button pops in with a ten-line custom transition in src/lib/motion/transitions.ts, and all of it reads its duration from the --dur-* tokens or from the one MediaQuery in src/lib/motion/prefers.svelte.ts. The hero is the exception that earns GSAP: an attachment — a function that receives an element and returns a cleanup — with four rules the comment states: nothing is hidden until JavaScript runs, nothing that has been seen is taken away, reduced motion means no motion, and it plays once. The second rule is the one a review found. On a first load the server’s hero is painted long before the JavaScript arrives, and the timeline then snapped the title, the lede and the image to nothing and faded them back — the sentence a visitor had started to read blinked out. So alreadySeen() asks two questions: is this a hydration (the root layout has not yet set data-hydrated), and has the browser painted (a first-contentful-paint entry exists)? Both yes, and the hero stays exactly as it is; the timeline plays when the hero arrives with a client-side navigation, as new elements nobody has seen. The copy and the image are found by data-hero-copy and data-hero-image, so the attachment does not know the markup, and the cleanup kills the timeline and clears the inline styles GSAP wrote. It is imported by the home route alone, so the library ships in that chunk and no other.

The feature cards need no timeline, so they get none. inview only decides *when*: it sets data-animate in the browser while the grid is still below the fold, and data-inview the first time it scrolls into view, and then disconnects its observer. The CSS does the motion — a 12px rise on --dur-5, each card 70ms after the one before through the --i the markup sets — and rule 1 lives in the selector: a card is hidden only under [data-animate], which the server never writes, so with JavaScript off every card is simply there. A grid already on screen when the script arrives skips the hiding step, and under reduced motion the whole block sits inside a media query that does not match. The list itself is a declaration tag — a {const} in the markup, beside the one loop that uses it — and the next chapter says what one is in full.

Why the list is a bare {const} and the icon a $derived one

A bare declaration tag is worked out once, when its block is created; one that wraps its value in $derived is worked out again whenever what it reads changes — the compiler turns the first into a plain const and the second into a derived signal. The list reads only messages, and the one thing that could change those is the language. A language switch loads a new page — the switcher’s links carry data-sveltekit-reload — and the new page works the list out afresh in the new language, so once is all it needs, and the comment above it says it is bare on purpose. Icon reads the loop’s item instead, and an item is like a prop: Svelte’s best practices say to “treat props as though they will change”, and to make a value that depends on one $derived. A keyed {#each} keeps a card whose key survives a change to the list and hands it the new item; a bare tag there would go on drawing the old icon. This list never changes, so the $derived costs nothing today, and it is the form that stays right on the day the list does.

Contrast, checked on every lint

Every ratio in this chapter — 5.36:1 for the tertiary ink on paper, 3.06:1 for a chosen segment’s edge, 10.39:1 for the globe’s hints — is printed by a script, not remembered. Because every colour is a token and most tokens are a light-dark() pair, whether text is readable is a question tokens.css can answer on its own, without a browser: parse it, resolve both sides of each pair and the var() aliases between tokens, and work out the WCAG ratio of every pair the design puts on top of each other.

That is the table the design promises, as data: every text ink on every surface tier, the fill ink on every stop kind, the focus ring on every paper, the segment edge on its track and on itself, and the accent and state colours where they are used as text. The floor is the standard’s — 4.5:1 for text, 3:1 for something that is not text but must be seen — and the maths is too: each channel linearised, weighted by how bright the eye finds it into a luminance, and the ratio of two luminances each plus 0.05. A pair whose token does not exist counts as a failure, so renaming --ink-3 cannot quietly drop its rows.

pnpm run lint ends with this script, so a token change that makes the tertiary ink unreadable on a card fails in a second, before a browser has started; --report prints the whole table, and scripts/screens.ts prints it again beside the screenshots. The module is pure — no DOM, no file system — so a script, a unit test (chapter 42) and the screenshot tool all import the same table.

Why a static table, when axe checks contrast in the browser

axe does check it, and chapter 43 runs axe on every screen in both themes. But axe can only judge what is on screen in the states the suite reaches: an error line inside a dialog, a warning chip, a hovered link may never be rendered there. The table checks every pair the design *promises*, in both themes, whether or not a page shows it today — and when it fails it names two tokens, which is where the fix goes, rather than a DOM node, which is where the symptom was. The two disagree only when a component puts colours together that the table does not list, and that is a conversation the design should have anyway.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain light-dark() and why the theme class only sets color-scheme.
  • You know why the boot script has a hash and no nonce.
  • You can state the four rules of the hero timeline, and say why the feature cards animate with CSS instead.
  • You can say how the hero fetches one print of two, and why the server has to know the theme for that.
  • You know which file a contrast ratio in this chapter comes from, and what fails when a token change breaks one.
